chapters.title: The Boy From the Railway House

blocks.text: Amancio Ortega Gaona was born on ==28 March 1936== in Busdongo de Arbas, a mountain village in the province of León, in northern Spain. Fortune magazine described it as a hamlet of about 60 people. He was the youngest of four children in a family with very little money.

Busdongo sits more than 1,200 metres up in the mountains, on the railway line that links the dry plateau of Castile with Asturias on the coast. In winter, heavy snow could cut the village off from the world. The Ortega family lived in a railway house built right beside the tracks.

photo.caption: Busdongo station after a snowfall, 2015. A future billionaire was born in this tiny railway village in 1936.
photo.author: VivirElTren.es

blocks.text: Born beside a railway line. Watch how trains steer his whole childhood.

The railway was the family's whole world. His father, Antonio Ortega, worked for the railways, and that job decided where the family lived. Some Spanish reports describe him as the head of Busdongo's little station, while others simply call him a railway worker.

His mother, Josefa Gaona, kept the home running. English-language profiles say she also worked as a housemaid, cleaning other people's houses to bring in money. Spanish reports describe the household as humble.

A railway wage was small. Drawing on his biographer, the French paper Le Petit Journal reported that local shopkeepers often had to let the Ortegas buy on credit. In plain words, the family bought food now and promised to pay later, when the next wage came in.
En casa no había nada de nada, pero nos educaron con valores.
blocks.who: Recollection quoted in Covadonga O'Shea's 2008 biography Así es Amancio Ortega, as reported by El Cronista

blocks.text: Translated, that line means: at home there was nothing at all, but they raised us with values. It comes from Así es Amancio Ortega, the 2008 book by the journalist Covadonga O'Shea. Her book was built on long conversations with Ortega himself and with his relatives, friends and colleagues, which makes it the closest thing we have to his own account.
A few weeks in the snow, then the Basque Country

The family did not stay in Busdongo for long. Diario de León says they left after only a few weeks, and other reports say Amancio was still a baby. His father's railway job moved them east to Tolosa, a small industrial town in Gipuzkoa, in Spain's Basque Country.

So the first home he could actually remember was not in León at all. It was Tolosa, where he spent his early childhood. The family stayed there until the railway transferred his father again, in ==1944==.

photo.caption: Tolosa, Gipuzkoa, in 1941. Amancio was about five, living here because of his father's railway posting.
photo.author: Vicente Martín (Foto Car collection, Kutxa Fototeka)

blocks.text: He was born in 1936, the year the Spanish Civil War began. Spanish accounts of his early life place it in the hard years after that war, when ordinary families like his had very little. A boy born in that time and place had no reason to expect anything special.

For example: Amancio Ortega and the Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa were born on exactly the same day, 28 March 1936. One became one of the most famous writers in the Spanish language. The other had, by 2013, become the third-richest person in the world, according to Fortune.
A new city by the sea

In 1944 the railway moved the family once more, this time to A Coruña. It is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Galicia, in the far north-west corner of Spain. This is where Amancio grew up, and it is the city he never really left.

Count the moves. Before he was nine, Amancio had lived in three very different corners of Spain: the snowy mountains of León, the Basque Country and the Atlantic coast of Galicia. Each move happened because a railway office somewhere decided where his father was needed. The boy learned early that his family had very little control over its own life.

In A Coruña the family lived in a row house that backed onto the train tracks, a home that doubled as housing for railway workers. Galicia had few jobs, and many of its men worked at sea. Remember that detail, because it matters later in this story.
Every move so far was decided by someone else's job.
The day at the shop counter

The scene that shaped his life happened at a shop counter. When Amancio was about 13, he stood beside his mother at a local store while she asked, once again, to buy on credit. This time the answer was no.
He heard someone say, 'Señora, I cannot give this to you. You have to pay for it.'
blocks.who: Covadonga O'Shea, his biographer, speaking to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: O'Shea told Fortune that the boy felt deeply humiliated. Le Petit Journal reported that this was one of the few childhood memories Ortega shared with her, and that he told her the moment had destroyed him. O'Shea's book came out in 2008, so he was in his seventies when he told her this story about being 13.

What he did next is the important part. He decided to start working, earn money and help his family, and he chose never to go back to school. O'Shea sees this moment as the root of the extreme work ethic that everyone who knows him describes.
Shame became fuel. Read this twice.

It would be easy to turn this into a movie scene where a poor boy swears to become a billionaire. But that is not what the sources say. __He did not set out to get rich. He set out to make sure his family never stood at that counter again.__ The fortune came later, as a side effect of solving that much smaller, much more personal problem.
School, briefly

Very little is reliably known about his classroom years. The Spanish news site Vozpópuli reports that at about 12 he was a pupil at a Colegio del Sagrado Corazón, a Catholic school, and that he left early, reportedly to help the family's finances. He never received any higher education.
Sources disagree on his exact age when he walked out of school for good. Some say 13, others say 14. Either way, he was still a child, and he has been working ever since.

For example: if Amancio had grown up in India today, he would have left school somewhere around Class 8. No board exams, no college applications, no degree. Everything he later knew about clothes, money and people, he learned on the job.

items.text: Born in Busdongo de Arbas, León, the youngest of four children of a railway employee.
A few weeks or months later, his father's railway job moves the family to Tolosa, in the Basque Country.
Early childhood in Tolosa. Money is so tight that shopkeepers often sell to the family on credit.
Another railway transfer takes the family to A Coruña, Galicia. They live in a railway row house by the tracks.
At about 13, he watches a shopkeeper refuse his mother credit. He decides to leave school and work.

blocks.text: No money, no degree, no contacts. Just a reason.

chapters.title: The Errand Boy Who Watched Everything

blocks.text: Around the age of 13 or 14, Amancio got his first job. He became a recadero, an errand boy, at Gala, a shirt shop in A Coruña. It was the bottom rung of the clothing trade, and it was where his real education began.

Gala made shirts for wealthy customers. As the delivery boy, Amancio carried the finished clothes through the streets and ran whatever errands the shop needed. It was humble work, and he took it because the family needed the money.

Amazingly, Gala was still trading on the same downtown corner in 2013. Its owner then, José Martínez, had inherited the shop from his father. Martínez and Amancio first became friends at Gala when they were both ==14 years old==.
No one ever comes in here to buy anything. They just want to know about Amancio.
blocks.who: José Martínez, owner of the Gala shirt shop and Ortega's teenage friend, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: Fortune gives us one lovely, ordinary picture of those teenage years. The two boys spent their afternoons folding shirts at Gala and then riding their bikes around town. No grand plans, no business school, just two teenagers doing their job and then going out.

Decades later, the little shirt shop became an odd kind of landmark. Martínez told Fortune that visitors came in not to buy shirts but to ask about the errand boy who had once worked there. The most famous thing Gala ever produced, it turned out, was not a shirt at all.
He was 14 here, folding other people's shirts.
What a delivery boy can see

A delivery job sounds boring, but it gave Amancio an unusual view of the whole business. After Gala he worked as an assistant to drapers and tailors, the people who sold cloth and made clothes to measure. Moving between these jobs, he watched how a piece of clothing travelled from the designer, to the workshop, to the shop, and finally to the customer.

He noticed something that most people in the trade simply accepted. Every time a garment passed from one set of hands to the next, its cost went up. The International Directory of Business Biographies says this lesson convinced him that the way to win was to get products to customers directly, without a chain of middlemen.

For example: think of a shirt's journey as a relay race. The cloth seller adds a margin, the tailor adds a margin, the shop adds a margin, and each handover takes time. Young Amancio was the runner who saw every handover, and he realised that a business owning the whole race could be both cheaper and faster.

Fortune reports that by the age of ==16==, he had reached a clear conclusion. The real money, he believed, was in giving customers exactly what they wanted, and giving it to them quickly. To do that, he would need to control the whole supply chain himself.
Sixteen years old. This idea later powered Zara's entire model.

__Most teenagers in a job only see their own small task. Amancio studied the whole system around him.__ That habit of watching, asking why things cost what they cost, and imagining a shorter path is the single most useful thing a young worker can copy from him.
La Maja: a family shop floor

His next big step was La Maja, a clothing and haberdashery shop in A Coruña. His older brother Antonio and his sister Josefa, known as Pepita, already worked there. Accounts differ on the timing: one Spanish report says he started there as an errand boy at 14, while others place his move after his years at Gala.

He started at the bottom again and earned the owners' trust. Over time he was promoted from errand boy to dependiente, a shop assistant serving customers at the counter. For a teenager who had left school, this was a real step up.

Behind that counter he picked up what El Español calls key knowledge about the business and about how customers behave. He saw which pieces people wanted, which they could not afford, and which sat unsold on the shelves. This was market research, years before he had a word for it.

Age by which he decided speed and control were the real money
Ortega children; Amancio was the youngest, and two siblings later joined his business

blocks.text: The girl from La Maja

La Maja is also where he met Rosalía Mera, the woman who would become his first wife and business partner. Rosalía was born in A Coruña in 1944, about eight years after Amancio. Her parents were factory workers.
Her story mirrors his. She left school at just ==11== to work as a sales assistant at La Maja. Like Amancio, she learned the clothing trade standing behind a shop counter, not sitting in a classroom.
Two kids who left school early. Together they'd build an empire.
The hunger

People who have studied his life keep coming back to one word. Blanco, one of the authors of an unauthorised biography of Ortega, told Fortune that poverty had given the young man a drive that never switched off.
There was a hunger.
blocks.who: Blanco, co-author of an unauthorised biography of Ortega, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: Spanish reports sum up those years in one simple line: he started working at 14 and has not stopped since. Put that next to the scene at the shop counter and you understand the teenager. He was not chasing status or fun. He was making sure the family was safe.
Almost nothing reliable survives about his teenage reading. We won't make it up.

items.text: Leaves school at 13 or 14 and starts as an errand boy at Gala, a shirt shop for wealthy clients.
Becomes friends with José Martínez, son of Gala's owner. They fold shirts and ride bikes together.
Works as an assistant to drapers and tailors, and sees costs rise at every step of a garment's journey.
Concludes that the money lies in giving customers what they want, fast, by controlling the supply chain.
Joins his siblings at La Maja, rises to shop assistant, and meets Rosalía Mera.

blocks.title: Your first job is a classroom
blocks.text: Amancio's first jobs paid very little, but he treated them like a free course in how his industry worked. Wherever you work at 16 or 19, a café, a shop, an internship, notice where the money goes, where time is wasted and what customers keep asking for. That notebook is your future business plan.

chapters.title: From Shop Counter to Kitchen Table

blocks.text: Amancio Ortega never went to university, and he had no formal higher education of any kind. His school was the shop floor. A Spanish profile sums up his start simply: he began in textiles at 14, working as a shop assistant in two well-known clothing stores.

Through the 1950s he kept climbing inside the trade. By the early 1960s he had become the manager of a local clothing shop. Spanish press accounts connect his rise with La Maja, the shop where his brother and sister worked.
No degree. Still running a shop in his mid-twenties.
The manager who noticed who wasn't buying
As manager, he saw a problem that sat in plain view. The garments in the shop were lovely, but only the wealthy people of the city could afford them. Everyone else looked, touched and walked away.
Very important for first-time founders! Look at who can't afford it.

So he started making cheaper versions himself. He bought less expensive fabric in Barcelona, cut the pieces by hand using patterns made of cardboard, and sold the finished clothes to local shops. It was a side project, built with his own hands and his own savings.

One product stood out: the quilted housecoat, or bata, worn at home by the well-off women of A Coruña. Working with his brother and sister, their partners and Rosalía, he made these housecoats and sold them for less than the competition. Later the family added men's shirts and sportswear.

For example: picture a smart quilted housecoat that only A Coruña's richer families could buy. The Ortegas made a similar one with cheaper cloth, hand-cut pieces and almost no overheads, then sold it below the shop price. Same look, lower price, and a whole new group of customers who could finally say yes.

This was not a factory yet. El Español reports that he and Rosalía began by making clothes from home. __The business behind thousands of stores around the world started as two shop workers making clothes at home.__
A family firm takes shape
The early business was a family affair, and everyone had a clear role. Amancio ran the design side. His brother Antonio led the commercial work of selling, and his sister Josefa kept the books.

Josefa's role was not a small one. El Español notes that she kept the company's accounts from the very beginning. In a tiny business with no investors and no safety net, the person who watches every peseta can decide whether the company lives or dies.
Design, sales, money. Every startup needs these three seats filled.
In ==1963==, at the age of 27, Amancio turned the side project into a real company: Confecciones GOA. The name hid a small joke. It was his own initials, Amancio Ortega Gaona, written backwards.
Amancio Ortega opens Confecciones GOA, a small dressmaking workshop.
blocks.who: Inditex's official company history, entry for 1963

blocks.text: The money to start came from the business itself. He used the profits from his cheaper copies to open his first factory in 1963. Forbes describes the start the same modest way: a small family company making clothes.

That matters more than it sounds. Inditex, today one of the biggest clothing companies in the world, still counts 1963 and this small workshop as its beginning. Forbes lists his fortune as self-made: there was no inheritance, no wealthy backer and no family company to take over, only the family he worked beside.

items.label: His age when he founded Confecciones GOA
The year Inditex itself counts as its beginning
Gap between GOA and the first Zara shop

blocks.text: The women of Galicia

Remember those Galician families where the men were away at sea? Amancio turned that into his workforce. Fortune reports that he began organising thousands of local women into sewing cooperatives, small groups who made the garments while GOA handled design and sales.

One of those workers, Mercedes López, started working for him at just 14, about the age he had been at Gala. Decades later, she told Fortune that the conditions had been good and that the boss was close to the people on the sewing floor.
We knew Amancio well. He was very close to the workers.
blocks.who: Mercedes López, who began sewing for GOA at 14, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: GOA's quilted bathrobes sold well, and the little firm grew. Fortune describes a thriving production of bathrobes for this first company. The boy who once carried other people's shirts now had a team making his own designs.
Partners in work and life

Rosalía Mera was part of the business from the very start. Reports at her death in 2013 said she and Ortega began by making women's bathrobes together. In ==1966==, three years after GOA was founded, the two married.

Think about who these founders were. He was a railway worker's son who left school at 13 or 14. She had left school at 11. Neither had a degree, a rich parent or an investor, yet between them they knew more about real customers than most fashion executives of the time.
No investors. No degrees. Just skill, family and customers.
Two blocks from where it began

GOA was the seed. Twelve years later, on ==9 May 1975==, the couple opened their own shop on the ground floor of numbers 64 and 66, Juan Flórez Street, in A Coruña. It stood just two blocks from Gala, the shirt shop where Amancio had started as an errand boy.
He wanted to call it Zorba, after the film Zorba the Greek. But a bar nearby already used that name, so he reused the letters already made for the sign to spell a new word. The shop became Zara.

photo.caption: The first Zara shop on Juan Flórez Street, A Coruña, photographed in 2012. It opened in 1975, two blocks from the shirt shop where Amancio began as an errand boy.
photo.author: Nemigo

blocks.text: Two blocks from where he delivered shirts as a boy. Two.

That shop is where the next part of this book begins. But almost every idea that made Zara famous was already present in these early years: watch the customer, cut out the middlemen, move fast and keep control of making the clothes. Ortega himself has always said he did not do it alone.
No he estado solo en esto y no merezco ningún reconocimiento más que el del trabajo y la fortuna de haberme rodeado de los mejores.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, quoted from Covadonga O'Shea's biography (via Europa Press)

blocks.text: In English, he is saying that he has not been alone in this, and that he deserves no credit except for the work and for the luck of surrounding himself with the best people. For him, those people started with a brother who sold, a sister who counted the money and a young woman from La Maja who sewed beside him.

items.text: Works his way up inside A Coruña's clothing trade, from errand boy to shop assistant.
Manages a local clothing shop and starts making cheaper copies of expensive garments with Barcelona fabric and cardboard patterns.
Founds Confecciones GOA at 27, a small workshop making quilted housecoats, with his siblings and Rosalía Mera.
Marries Rosalía Mera, his partner in the business.
Opens the first Zara shop at Juan Flórez 64–66, A Coruña, two blocks from Gala.

blocks.title: Start with the customer who is being left out
blocks.text: Amancio's first product was not a new invention. It was a copy of something the rich already wore, made cheap enough for everyone else. Look around your own city for things people want but cannot afford, and ask what would have to change to bring the price down.

blocks.title: Fund the first step with the business itself
blocks.text: He had no investors. He made and sold a few pieces, kept the profit, and used it to build the next step. A small business that pays for itself from day one teaches you more, and owes less, than a big idea waiting for funding.

factCheck.method: Each claim was checked against pages read in full during research: Fortune's 2013 profile (which interviewed his biographer Covadonga O'Shea, the unauthorised biographer Blanco, his teenage friend José Martínez and early worker Mercedes López), Spanish press (El Español, Diario de León, El Cronista, Vozpópuli, El Debate/EFE, Libre Mercado, Europa Press, Forbes España), Le Petit Journal's 2013 piece on O'Shea's account, 2013 obituaries of Rosalía Mera (Il Post, The Local, DPA), Gale's International Directory of Business Biographies, Inditex's official history and the Forbes profile. Where sources gave different ages or dates, the text says so and the conflict is listed below. Wikipedia was used only to find leads. Several stronger sources (El País, El Mundo, La Voz de Galicia, ABC, El Norte de Castilla, La Opinión A Coruña, the Telegraph, Bloomberg, BBC) could not be opened from the research environment, so details found only in them were dropped. Photos come from Wikimedia Commons, with author and licence taken from the Commons API.

disputed.claim: The family moved to A Coruña in 1944.
disputed.note: Le Petit Journal and El Cronista give 1944. El Español says he was raised in A Coruña from age 12 (about 1948). Fortune (2013) says he moved there with his father's railway job at 14. The text uses 1944, which has two sources and fits the 'small boy' wording in Fortune.

disputed.claim: He was about 13 when a shopkeeper refused his mother credit.
disputed.note: Fortune (citing O'Shea) says 13. Some Spanish wire coverage of O'Shea's book says about 12. The text says 'about 13'.

disputed.claim: He left school and took his first job at 13 or 14.
disputed.note: Gale's directory and Le Petit Journal say 13; El Español and the Fortune friendship detail point to 14. The text gives both.

El Cronista and other Spanish reports call him head of the Busdongo station; Fortune, Vozpópuli and El Español just say railway worker. Diario de León calls him a 'ferroviario de Renfe', but RENFE was only created in 1941, so that label is loose for 1936. The text says 'worked for the railways' and notes the station-chief version.

disputed.claim: His mother worked as a housemaid.
disputed.note: Fortune and Gale say housemaid; Vozpópuli calls her a housewife (ama de casa). Her first name is given as Josefa (Vozpópuli) and Josefina (El Español). The text uses Josefa and says English-language profiles describe her as a housemaid.

disputed.claim: How long the family stayed in Busdongo.
disputed.note: Diario de León says a few weeks; Spanish Wikipedia (citing La Opinión A Coruña, which could not be opened) says about three months; El Cronista says he was still a baby. The text says 'a few weeks or months'.

Vozpópuli says he started at La Maja as an errand boy at 14; other accounts (El Español, Fortune, Gale) put the Gala shirt shop first, and Spanish Wikipedia leads say he moved to La Maja at 17. The text puts Gala first and flags the conflict.

disputed.claim: He attended a Colegio del Sagrado Corazón.
disputed.note: Vozpópuli places this at about age 12 without naming the city clearly; Spanish Wikipedia places the Sagrado Corazón school in Tolosa. The text names the school but not the city.

disputed.claim: Wording of the O'Shea family quote.
disputed.note: El Cronista's article body gives 'nos educaron con valores' while its headline and caption say 'en valores'. The text uses the body wording. The quote is reported as coming from O'Shea's 2008 book; the book text itself was not available.
The Local says so, but the Inditex holding company was created in 1985 (El Español). The text says she was part of the business from the start (GOA, 1963), not that she founded Inditex in 1963.
